catalog_quote: [Thomas 1916, Pt. III Timne Grammar, sec. 7 'Stress', p. ix] The stress usually falls on the first syllable of a word, exclusive of prefixes; the incidence is not changed by a suffix. There are a few exceptions such as kabalai, basket; kara, scrape off. In the case of nouns with inseparable prefixes the first syllable takes the stress, as the vowel is properly part of the word, though normally no Timne word begins with a vowel, pronouns excepted. Where a noun is associated with a word that may be a verb or an adjective, the main stress falls on the verb in the first case, on the noun in the second. [sec. 8 'Tones'] The role of tones in Timne is comparatively small, owing largely, no doubt, to the part played by prefixes in distinguishing the homophones. Among words distinguished by tones may be cited: bi, hole; bi, black ... [Schlenker 1864 sec. 11, pp. 24-25] 1) The stress of the voice…

tone_statements.citation: Kanu, Sullay M. & Benjamin V. Tucker. 2010. Temne. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 40(2): 247-253 (Illustrations of the IPA). doi:10.1017/S002510031000006X
tone_statements.quote: As stated earlier, Temne is a tonal language (Wilson 1968, Nemer & Mountford 1984). According to Kamarah (1994) and Dalby (1966), Temne has high, low, rising and falling tones. Based on our data and investigation of tone, we have found no indication of contour tones and thus support Wilson (1968, 2007), who argues for only high and low tones in Temne. Tone fulfils both lexical and grammatical functions in the language. The examples below illustrate words that are lexically contrastive. Tone is used to make grammatical distinctions such as definiteness and past tense.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: 2 level tones H, L (no contours per authors; others posit R, F); lexical and grammatical tone; downdrift and downstep.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding quotations (Thomas 1916 sec. 7-8, p. ix; Schlenker 1864 sec. 11, pp. 24-27) are present verbatim at the stated scanned locators in the copies we hold; the Kanu & Tucker 2010 sentence is also confirmed. (2) Deciding source: two pre-modern primary grammars (1864 missionary reference grammar with an 'Accentuation' chapter; 1916 grammar sketch that treats stress and tone in separate sections), consistent with each other and explicit that prefixes are excluded and suffixes inert, so the set by morphology (stem-initial) reading is faithful to them. (3) But they are not the best available descriptions: Glottolog lists a dedicated phonology dissertation (Kamarah 1994, 223 pp), a modern Lincom reference grammar (Kamarah 2007, 167 pp) and Yillah 1992 (CUNY, phonology and morphology), none. Everything modern that is open and was downloaded now (Dalby 1966 JWAL, Wilson 1968 JWAL

sources.citation: Kanu, Sullay Mohamed. 2012. Valence-Increasing Morphology in Temne. PhD dissertation, University of Alberta (369 pp).
sources.quote: 'Temne is a tonal language, having a high tone ... and a low tone'; tone lexical (bi 'hole' vs bi 'black') and grammatical (definiteness); only H and L basic tones (contours from coalescence). The word 'stress' occurs nowhere in the dissertation (a full-text search for stress/accent count 0).

sources.citation: Wilson, W. A. A. 1968. An interpretation of the Temne tone system. Journal of West African Languages 5(1): 5-11.
sources.quote: 'Temne can be characterized as having a terraced-level system of tones ... two tonal phonemes, Low and High, and a juncture phoneme of Downstep.' Only mention of stress is phrasal: 'the beginning of the main clause predicate is signalled by some form of stress on the first H tone ... This would need to be verified.' Nothing on word stress.

sources.citation: Dalby, David. 1966. Lexical analysis in Temne with an illustrative word list. Journal of West African Languages 3(2): 5-26.
sources.quote: 'Tonology has been neglected almost entirely in previous studies of the language, even though tone plays a most important lexical and morphological role'; six tone-marks, downstep, downslide, upstep. No occurrence of 'stress' or 'accent' in 22 pages.

sources.note: Section 'Tone': Temne is a tonal language; the authors find no contour tones and side with Wilson (1968, 2007) for only High and Low tones, against Kamarah 1994 and Dalby 1966 (H, L, rising, falling); tone is lexically contrastive and marks grammatical categories (definite vs indefinite nouns of the ɛ- class by H vs L on the class affix; past tense); downdrift (HLH) and downstep (HH) both occur; they call for acoustic study of tone. Audio-illustrated word list and passage.

sources.note: Per Kanu 2012 (Valence-increasing morphology in Temne, PhD Alberta, sec. 2.1.2, pp. 30-31; a work listed here, copy): 'Reference to tonal constrast has been made by Dalby (1966), Kanu (2002) and Kamarah (1994) who claim that there are also rising and falling tones in Temne' -- so the 2002 MA thesis treats Temne tonal contrast and posits contour (rising/falling) tones in addition to H and L, the position Kanu & Tucker 2010 later rejected in favour of H/L only (contours arising from vowel coalescence of affix tones). Also cited by Kanu & Tucker 2010 for the /Vj/ diphthong convention.
